Make sure they have been working on Creed memorization from Session 0.6 throughout. Recommended video: Search Orthodox Study Bible overview or How to read the Bible Orthodox way — Ancient Faith has content on lectio divina in the Orthodox tradition.
key_concepts: Read Scripture within the Church, not alone — The first principle of Orthodox biblical reading is that Scripture belongs to the community. When you read the Bible alone you bring your own assumptions, your own emotional state, your own limited understanding. When you read within the Church — hearing it proclaimed in the Liturgy, reading the Fathers' commentaries, praying the Psalms with the community — you are protected from your own blind spots and connected to two thousand years of faithful interpretation.

Read Scripture through the lens of Christ — Every passage of the Old Testament and the New must be read in light of who Christ is and what He has done. This does not mean forcing every verse to be about Jesus in an obvious way. It means reading with the awareness that all of Scripture is one story — the story of God pursuing His people — and Christ is the destination of that story. The Incarnation, Cross, and Resurrection are the interpretive key to everything.

Read Scripture with the Church Fathers — When you encounter a difficult passage, the Orthodox instinct is to ask: what did the Fathers say? Not because the Fathers are infallible but because they were closer to the Apostles, they were immersed in the living Tradition, they often read in the original Greek, and the Church has tested and affirmed their interpretations over centuries. The Orthodox Study Bible is a good starting point — its notes draw on patristic commentary throughout.

The lectionary — Scripture in liturgical rhythm — The Orthodox Church reads the New Testament in its entirety over the course of the liturgical year through the lectionary — the assigned Epistle and Gospel readings for each Sunday and feast day. This means that year after year, generation after generation, Orthodox Christians hear the same passages at the same times, shaped by the same liturgical context. This communal rhythm is itself a form of interpretation.

The Psalms — the prayer book of the Church — The 150 Psalms of the Psalter are the backbone of all Orthodox liturgical prayer. They are prayed at Vespers, Matins, the Hours, and the Liturgy. Monastics chant the entire Psalter every week. Beginning to pray the Psalms — even just one or two regularly — connects you to the oldest continuous prayer tradition in the world, used by both Israel and the Church for three thousand years.

Lectio Divina — slow, prayerful reading — The ancient monastic practice of lectio divina — divine reading — is a way of reading Scripture not for information but for encounter. You read slowly, perhaps only a few verses. You read again. You let a word or phrase that strikes you stay with you. You pray it. You sit in silence. This is not mysticism — it is the natural way of reading a text you believe is the living Word of God rather than mere historical information.
sessions.reading_note: John 1:1–18 was chosen as the capstone reading for Topic 1 because it is itself a meditation on what Scripture is and what the Word of God means. In the beginning was the Word — John begins exactly as Genesis begins, connecting the entire sweep of Scripture in one phrase. The Word was God. The Word became flesh. Scripture is the written form of the eternal Word of God who became human in Jesus Christ. Reading John 1 slowly, with the awareness of everything your child has learned in this topic, is a fitting culmination — the Word reading about the Word.
sessions.discussion_q1: You wrote your own personal rule for reading the Bible as an Orthodox Christian. Read it to me. What is the principle you feel most strongly about and why?
sessions.discussion_q2: You practiced lectio divina with John 1:1–14. What word or phrase stayed with you? What prayer did you write? Tell me about the experience — was it different from how you usually read?
sessions.discussion_q3: We have spent five sessions on Scripture and Holy Tradition. What is the single most important thing you learned in this topic? What has changed about how you think about the Bible?
sessions.journal_prompt: In your Field Manual, write your own rule for reading the Bible as an Orthodox Christian. Based on what you have learned in this whole topic — all five sessions — write at least five principles that should guide how you read Scripture. Make it personal. This is your rule, not a textbook answer.
sessions.family_activity: As a family, look up the Orthodox lectionary for next Sunday — the assigned Epistle and Gospel readings. Read them together at home before you go to church. Then at the Liturgy, listen for those same passages. After church, talk about what you heard differently having already read them at home. This is how the lectionary is meant to work.
sessions.personal_activity: Practice lectio divina with John 1:1–14 this week. Read it slowly, once. Read it again. Write in your Field Manual the one word or phrase that stayed with you — not the most theologically important one, but the one that actually struck you personally. Then write a short prayer based on that word or phrase. This is the oldest form of Christian Bible reading.
sessions.reading_reference: John 1:1–18 — In the Beginning Was the Word
sessions.liturgical_connection: This Sunday is your family's first chance to practice the lectionary activity from this session. Look up the readings before you go to church, read them at home together, and then listen for them in the Liturgy. After the service, ask your child: what did you notice? What did you hear differently? This is not a homework assignment — it is an invitation to participate in how Orthodox Christians have been hearing Scripture for two thousand years.

sessions.title: The Apostolic Age — From Jerusalem to the World
sessions.description: On the day of Pentecost, fifty days after the Resurrection, a small group of frightened disciples locked in an upper room in Jerusalem became the Church. Fire descended. Languages multiplied. Three thousand people were baptized in a single day. And then they went. Peter went to Rome. Andrew went to Greece and to what is now Ukraine. Thomas went all the way to India. John stayed in Ephesus. Matthew went to Ethiopia. The faith of the Resurrection — this explosive, uncontainable news that God had entered human history, died, and risen from the dead — could not be kept in one room or one city or one culture. Within a single generation the Gospel had reached the edges of the known world. The Apostolic Age is not ancient history. It is the moment the Church you belong to was born and sent.
sessions.parent_note: The Apostolic Age is where the entire story of the Church begins and where the Orthodox Church's claim to continuity is rooted. The most important concept to reinforce is Apostolic Succession — the unbroken chain of ordination from the Apostles to today. This is the reason why the Eucharist your family receives is valid, why absolution in Confession is real, why the chrism at Baptism conveys the Holy Spirit. The sacraments work because the chain is unbroken. St. Paul's conversion is one of the most dramatic narratives in all of human history. A man who held the coats of those who stoned St. Stephen became the man who wrote more of the New Testament than anyone else. Do not rush past that. Recommended video: Search Acts of the Apostles Orthodox or Apostolic Age early Church — Ancient Faith Radio has an excellent series on the early Church.
key_concepts: Pentecost — the birthday of the Church — Fifty days after Pascha, the Holy Spirit descended on the gathered disciples as tongues of fire. St. Peter stood and preached the first Christian sermon. Three thousand people believed and were baptized. The Church was born not as a private spiritual experience but as a public community, gathered, Spirit-filled, and immediately growing. Every year on Pentecost Sunday the Orthodox Church celebrates this birthday.

The Apostles went everywhere — The Apostles did not stay in Jerusalem. They scattered across the known world carrying the Gospel. Five ancient patriarchates mark where the faith took root: Constantinople — the New Rome and center of the Christian empire. Alexandria — founded by St. Mark, home of the great theologians. Antioch — where followers of Christ were first called Christians. Jerusalem — the mother Church. Rome — where Peter and Paul both died as martyrs. These five sees formed the structure of the early Church.

St. Paul — the Apostle to the Gentiles — Saul of Tarsus was a Pharisee who persecuted the Church until Christ appeared to him on the road to Damascus. Blinded by the light, he was baptized and became Paul — the most tireless missionary in Christian history. He planted churches across Asia Minor, Greece, and Rome. His letters form the theological backbone of the New Testament. He was martyred in Rome around 67 AD.

The Apostolic Fathers — those who knew the Apostles — After the Apostles came men who had known them personally. St. Ignatius of Antioch — third bishop of Antioch, wrote seven letters on his way to be martyred in Rome. St. Polycarp of Smyrna — disciple of St. John the Apostle. St. Clement of Rome — knew Peter and Paul personally. These men are the living link between the Apostles and the wider Church.

The faith spread through ordinary people — Not only bishops and famous missionaries carried the Gospel. Merchants, soldiers, slaves, and travelers brought the faith wherever they went. A Christian merchant settling in a new city, a slave converted by her master, a soldier stationed in a distant province — all of these ordinary lives became vehicles of the Gospel.

The Orthodox Church traces itself directly to the Apostles — Every Orthodox bishop today can trace an unbroken chain of ordination back through history to the Apostles themselves. This is not a claim about institutional prestige. It is the guarantee that the faith and the sacraments your family receives are the same ones Christ gave to His Apostles.
sessions.reading_note: Acts 2 was chosen because it is the foundational moment — the birth of the Church in time. Peter's proclamation, the crowd's response, the command to repent and be baptized, and the immediate formation of a community devoted to the Apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer. These four marks describe exactly what the Orthodox Church does every Sunday. Your child is reading the blueprint of the service they attend each week.
sessions.discussion_q1: What happened on Pentecost? Why does the Orthodox Church call it the birthday of the Church? What changed that day?
sessions.discussion_q2: You found out which Apostle or saint brought the faith to your part of the world. Tell me what you discovered. What surprised you?
sessions.discussion_q3: The session says the faith spread through ordinary people — merchants, slaves, soldiers. What does that tell you about how the faith spreads today? What does it mean for your own life?
sessions.journal_prompt: In your Field Manual, draw a simple map of the Mediterranean world and mark where at least five Apostles went after Pentecost. Then answer this question: what does it mean for your own life that the faith traveled all the way from Jerusalem to where you live today?
sessions.family_activity: As a family, read Acts 2:1–47 together — the full Pentecost account. Read it as a story, not a lesson. Then discuss: if you had been in Jerusalem that day and heard Peter preach, what do you think you would have done? What made three thousand people respond in a single day?
sessions.personal_activity: Find out which Apostle or saint is traditionally credited with bringing the Gospel to your part of the world — or to Greece if your family has Greek heritage. Look up one detail about that mission and write it in your Field Manual. You are connected to that saint through an unbroken chain.
sessions.reading_reference: Acts 2:1–12, 36–42 — The Day the Church Was Born
sessions.liturgical_connection: This Sunday at the Liturgy, listen for the commemoration of the Apostles — they are mentioned throughout. In the Anaphora the priest commemorates the Theotokos and specifically the Apostles. Also notice that the Epistle reading is always from the New Testament letters — most written by St. Paul. Every Sunday your family hears the voice of an Apostle. Point this out to your child and ask them to listen as if hearing it for the first time.

sessions.title: Persecution & The Early Church
sessions.description: For nearly three hundred years, to be a Christian was to risk everything. The Roman Empire — the most powerful government the ancient world had ever seen — occasionally turned its full machinery of violence against the followers of Christ. Men and women were thrown to lions. They were burned alive. They were beheaded. They were tortured and given every opportunity to simply say two words — Caesar is Lord — and walk free. Almost none of them did. The blood of the martyrs, wrote Tertullian, is the seed of the Church. He was right. Every wave of persecution produced more Christians, not fewer. The faith that could not be killed by Rome could not be killed by anything. And the martyrs — whose names fill the Orthodox calendar, whose relics rest beneath every Orthodox altar — are still interceding for us today.
sessions.parent_note: The persecutions are not comfortable material for children — and they should not be made comfortable. The faith your family practices was purchased at enormous cost. Children in this age range are capable of understanding sacrifice and they are deeply moved by real stories of real courage. Do not sanitize the martyrs. Let St. Polycarp be 86 years old and refuse to deny Christ. Let St. Ignatius beg his friends not to rescue him because he wants to be ground by the lions for Christ. These are not horror stories — they are love stories. The most important pastoral question to raise with your child: if faith is worth dying for, what does that tell us about how worth living for it is? Recommended video: Search Orthodox martyrs early Church or St. Ignatius of Antioch — Ancient Faith has good material.
key_concepts: Why Rome persecuted Christians — The Roman Empire was generally tolerant of different religions. What made Christians dangerous in Roman eyes was their exclusivity — they refused to worship the Roman gods, refused to offer incense to the emperor's image, and refused to say Caesar is Lord. In a society where religion and civic life were inseparable, this made Christians appear to be enemies of the state. They were accused of atheism (refusing the gods), cannibalism (misunderstanding the Eucharist), and political subversion.

The ten great persecutions — Christian tradition numbers ten major Roman persecutions, beginning under Emperor Nero in 64 AD — who blamed Christians for the great fire of Rome — and ending under Emperor Diocletian in 303 AD, the most severe of all. Between these, emperors came and went, persecution intensified and relaxed, but the threat never entirely disappeared for nearly three centuries.

The martyrs — witnesses unto death — The Greek word martys means witness. A martyr is someone whose death is itself a testimony — a witness to the reality of the Resurrection. Orthodox Christians do not believe the martyrs simply died bravely. They believe the martyrs died in the power of the Risen Christ, sustained by Him in their final moments. This is why their deaths were recorded, their relics preserved, and their feast days celebrated. They are not dead — they are alive in Christ.

St. Ignatius of Antioch — the wheat of God — On his way to be executed in Rome around 107 AD, St. Ignatius wrote seven letters to churches along the route. He begged the Roman Christians not to intervene and save him. He wrote: I am the wheat of God and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts that I may be found pure bread of Christ. He was devoured by lions in the Colosseum. His feast day is October 17.

The Edict of Milan 313 AD — the end of persecution — Emperor Constantine — who tradition says saw a cross in the sky before a decisive battle with the words In this sign conquer — became the first Christian emperor. In 313 AD he issued the Edict of Milan granting religious tolerance throughout the empire. Christians could practice their faith openly for the first time. Churches were built. Property was returned. The era of persecution ended.

Relics — the bodies of those who died for Christ — Every Orthodox altar contains the relics of a saint or martyr. This is not superstition — it is theology. The body of a martyr is sacred because it was a temple of the Holy Spirit, because it suffered for Christ, and because it will be raised in glory at the Resurrection. When you stand at the altar for the Eucharist you are standing above the remains of someone who died rather than deny the faith.
sessions.reading_note: Revelation 2:8–11 was chosen because it is Christ's own word to the church at Smyrna — the church of St. Polycarp — commanding them to be faithful unto death. Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Be faithful unto death and I will give you the crown of life. This passage was almost certainly read aloud in the church Polycarp led. When he refused to deny Christ before the Roman proconsul, he was living out this specific command from the Risen Lord to his specific community.
sessions.discussion_q1: Why did Rome persecute Christians specifically? What was it about Christianity that the empire found threatening?
sessions.discussion_q2: You looked up a martyr this week. Tell me who they were and what they said. What do you think gave them that courage?
sessions.discussion_q3: St. Ignatius said he wanted to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts for Christ. That sounds extreme to us. What does it tell you about what he believed? What would you have to believe to feel that way?
sessions.journal_prompt: In your Field Manual, write a short letter from the perspective of a Christian living in Rome during the persecution of Diocletian. You know that being found out could mean death. What do you write? What do you believe? What gives you the courage to continue?
sessions.family_activity: As a family, read the martyrdom of St. Polycarp together — his final words to the Roman proconsul when ordered to deny Christ. The account is short and available on any Orthodox saints website. He said: Eighty-six years I have served Him and He has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me? Discuss: what gives a person that kind of certainty? How does your family build that kind of faith now, before it is tested?
sessions.personal_activity: Look up the feast day of one martyr on the Orthodox calendar — any martyr you choose. Read a brief account of how they died and what they said. Write one sentence in your Field Manual that they spoke or that you will remember about them. Then write: what would it take to have that kind of faith?
sessions.liturgical_connection: This Sunday before the Liturgy, look at the altar. Somewhere beneath or within it are the relics of a saint — this is required by Orthodox canon law. Every Liturgy is celebrated over the body of someone who died for the faith. Point this out to your child quietly before the service begins. After, ask them: how does knowing that change the way the Liturgy feels?

sessions.title: The Ecumenical Councils — Defining the Faith
sessions.description: Imagine the most important question anyone has ever asked — who is Jesus Christ? Not just a good teacher? Not just a prophet? The Church had always believed He was God. But how? In what sense? With what relationship to the Father? And if He was truly God — was He also truly human? Could God actually be born, suffer, and die? Beginning in the fourth century, these questions exploded into open controversy. Whole cities took sides. Emperors intervened. Bishops were exiled. And out of this fire — in seven great councils spread across five centuries — the Church hammered out the precise language of what Christians believe about God and about Christ. The Seven Ecumenical Councils are not ancient bureaucratic meetings. They are the moments when the Holy Spirit guided the Church to say, clearly and permanently, what has always been true.
sessions.parent_note: The Councils can feel like ancient church politics to children who do not understand what was at stake. The key is to make the stakes clear. If Arius was right — if Christ was a creature and not truly God — then the Eucharist is not the Body and Blood of God, salvation is not union with God, and the whole Orthodox understanding of theosis collapses. Everything depends on who Christ actually is. The Councils were not about winning arguments. They were about preserving the possibility of salvation. The Chalcedonian definition — one Person in two natures — is worth spending real time on. The four negative words are the key: without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. The Sunday of Orthodoxy is the most direct liturgical connection to the Councils and is worth attending with your child if at all possible. Recommended video: Search Seven Ecumenical Councils Orthodox — Ancient Faith has several good series.
key_concepts: What is an Ecumenical Council? — An Ecumenical Council is a gathering of bishops from across the entire Church — ecumenical means worldwide — convened to address a matter of faith or practice affecting the whole body. The Orthodox Church recognizes seven Ecumenical Councils, from Nicea in 325 to Nicea II in 787. Their decisions are considered binding — not because bishops are infallible individually but because the whole Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, receives their definitions as true.

The First Council of Nicea, 325 AD — Is Christ truly God? — The heresy of Arius claimed that the Son of God was a created being — the greatest of all creatures, but still a creature. Against Arius, the Council of Nicea declared that the Son is homoousios — of one essence — with the Father. Not similar, not like, but the same essence. The Nicene Creed we recite every Sunday was born at this Council.

The First Council of Constantinople, 381 AD — Is the Holy Spirit truly God? — After Nicea settled the question of the Son, a new heresy arose denying the full divinity of the Holy Spirit. The First Council of Constantinople completed the Nicene Creed by adding the article on the Holy Spirit — who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified.

The Council of Ephesus, 431 AD — Is Mary truly the Theotokos? — The heresy of Nestorius claimed that Mary was only the mother of the human Christ — Christotokos — not the mother of God. The Council of Ephesus declared that Mary is truly Theotokos — God-bearer — because the one she bore is one Person, fully divine and fully human. When the council's decision was announced, the people of Ephesus carried the bishops through the streets by torchlight.

The Council of Chalcedon, 451 AD — Two natures, one Person — The Council of Chalcedon defined the most precise language about Christ: one Person in two natures — divine and human — without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. This Chalcedonian definition remains the standard of Orthodox Christology.

The Seventh Council, Nicea II, 787 AD — In defense of icons — The final Ecumenical Council addressed the Iconoclast controversy. The Council of Nicea II declared that the veneration of icons is legitimate and Orthodox because icons of Christ are possible precisely because He became truly human. To deny icons is to deny the Incarnation. This Council is celebrated on the Sunday of Orthodoxy every year.
sessions.reading_note: John 1:1–14 was chosen because it is the primary biblical text behind the Nicene definition. In the beginning was the Word — co-eternal with the Father, not created. The Word was God — not a lesser divine being but fully God. And the Word became flesh — the Incarnation that makes icons possible and salvation real. Colossians 1:15–20 adds Paul's majestic Christological hymn which the Arians tried to use in their favor and which the Council of Nicea definitively interpreted in the Orthodox sense.
sessions.discussion_q1: Name three of the Seven Ecumenical Councils and tell me the main question each one answered. Which one do you think was most important and why?
sessions.discussion_q2: You went through the Nicene Creed line by line this week. Which line means more to you now than it did before? What council or controversy is behind it?
sessions.discussion_q3: If Arius had won at Nicea — if the Church had accepted that Jesus was a created being and not truly God — what would be different about Christianity today? What would be lost?
sessions.journal_prompt: In your Field Manual, create a timeline of the Seven Ecumenical Councils — date, location, and the main question each one answered. Then write: why does it matter that the Church spent five centuries defining these things precisely? What would happen if they had not?
sessions.family_activity: As a family, attend the Sunday of Orthodoxy Liturgy at the beginning of Great Lent if you are able — this is the annual celebration of the Seventh Council and the restoration of icons. If that is not possible, read the Synodikon of Orthodoxy together — the declaration read on that Sunday — which begins: as the prophets beheld, as the apostles taught. It is one of the great texts of the Orthodox faith.
sessions.personal_activity: This week, recite the Nicene Creed slowly — line by line — and for each major statement, identify which Council or controversy it came from. Use what you learned in this session. Write in your Field Manual: which line of the Creed now means more to you than it did before, and why.
sessions.reading_reference: John 1:1–14 + Colossians 1:15–20 — Christ, the Eternal Word Made Flesh
sessions.liturgical_connection: This Sunday, recite the Nicene Creed with new awareness. Every line was defended at the cost of exile, controversy, and in some cases death. When you say we believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all ages, light of light, true God of true God, begotten not created, of one essence with the Father — you are reciting the victory of Nicea over Arianism. Point each phrase out to your child and name what it is defending.

sessions.title: The Great Schism — When the Church Divided
sessions.description: For a thousand years there was one Church. From Jerusalem to Rome, from Alexandria to Antioch, from Constantinople to the newly baptized Slavic nations — one Eucharist, one faith, one baptism. Then, on July 16, 1054, Cardinal Humbert of Rome walked into the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople — the greatest church in the world — and placed a letter of excommunication on the altar during the Divine Liturgy. The Patriarch of Constantinople responded by excommunicating the Cardinal. And the Church that had survived three centuries of Roman persecution, seven Ecumenical Councils, and countless heresies — split. The Great Schism of 1054 is not just a historical event. It is a wound that has not fully healed. And understanding what happened and why matters for every Orthodox Christian living in the Western world today.
sessions.parent_note: The Great Schism requires pastoral sensitivity. Many Orthodox families have Catholic relatives. Many Orthodox children have Protestant classmates. The goal of this session is not to produce children who are contemptuous of other Christians but children who understand their own tradition clearly and hold it with conviction and charity. The Orthodox position is not that Catholics and Protestants are damned or that they have no connection to Christ. It is that the fullness of the Apostolic faith is preserved in the Orthodox Church and that the divisions of 1054 and 1517 were genuine losses for all of Christianity. The Filioque is worth explaining carefully to your child — not as a technical detail but as a principle. No single church, not even Rome, has the authority to change the Creed that was defined by an Ecumenical Council of the whole Church. Recommended video: Search Great Schism 1054 Orthodox — Ancient Faith and Orthodox Wiki have good accessible material.
key_concepts: The five patriarchates and the rise of Rome — The early Church was governed by five ancient patriarchates of roughly equal honor: Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem. Rome had a primacy of honor as the see of Peter and the capital of the empire. But Rome began to claim a primacy of jurisdiction — the right to govern and overrule the other churches — that the East never accepted. This tension built for centuries before 1054.

The Filioque — the theological fault line — The Nicene Creed originally stated that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. In the Western church, the phrase and the Son (filioque in Latin) was gradually added. The East rejected this as a unilateral change to a Creed defined by an Ecumenical Council, which no single church had the authority to alter. This was not merely a political dispute — it reflected different understandings of the Trinity and of church authority.

What actually happened in 1054 — The excommunications of 1054 were technically between the papal legate Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius of Constantinople. The mutual excommunications were formally lifted in 1964 by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras. But full communion has not been restored because the underlying issues — the Filioque, papal supremacy, and other doctrinal matters — remain unresolved.

The Crusades — deepening the wound — The Fourth Crusade of 1204 was the event that made reunion nearly impossible for centuries. Western Crusaders instead sacked Constantinople — the heart of Eastern Christendom. They looted the Hagia Sophia, installed a Latin bishop, and established a Latin Empire. Orthodox Christians do not forget 1204. It remains a defining trauma.

What Orthodoxy says about Rome — The Orthodox Church does not say that Roman Catholics are not Christians or that their sacraments are entirely without grace. But the Orthodox Church does hold that the Bishop of Rome has no authority over other churches, that the Filioque is an unacceptable addition to the Creed, and that the reunion dialogues have not yet resolved these fundamental issues.

Living as Orthodox in a Western world — Most Orthodox Christians in America and Western Europe live surrounded by Protestant and Catholic Christianity. Understanding the Great Schism helps them understand both their differences from Western Christianity and why those differences matter. The Orthodox Church is not simply an older ethnic version of Catholicism. It is the Church of the Seven Councils, which has preserved the Apostolic faith without the additions Rome introduced and without the subtractions the Reformation made.
sessions.reading_note: John 17:20–23 — Christ's high priestly prayer for unity — was chosen because it frames the Great Schism in its proper theological context. Christ prayed that they may all be one as you, Father, are in me and I in you. Orthodox theology understands Christian unity not as institutional merger or lowest-common-denominator agreement but as unity in the truth. The Schism is a tragedy precisely because it fractures what Christ prayed for. This passage also guards against a triumphalist reading of Orthodoxy — the Orthodox Church longs for reunion, not merely for vindication.
sessions.discussion_q1: What were the two main causes of the Great Schism? Which do you think was more fundamental — the theological issue or the political issue?
sessions.discussion_q2: You looked at the Hagia Sophia this week. What did you feel looking at it? What does it mean to you that the schism happened in that building during the Divine Liturgy?
sessions.discussion_q3: Christ prayed that they may all be one. The Church is visibly divided. How should an Orthodox Christian feel about that? What does Christian unity mean if it cannot mean pretending the differences do not exist?
sessions.journal_prompt: In your Field Manual, write your answer to this question: the Orthodox Church holds that it is the one holy catholic and apostolic Church — and yet the Church is visibly divided. How do you hold these two things together? What does it mean for Orthodoxy to long for reunion while also believing it has preserved the fullness of the faith?
sessions.family_activity: As a family, discuss: you probably know Catholics and Protestants — neighbors, classmates, relatives, coworkers. How does understanding the Great Schism change how you think about them? How does the Orthodox Church hold together a belief in the fullness of the faith with a genuine love for other Christians and a genuine desire for unity?
sessions.personal_activity: Look up the Hagia Sophia — the great church in Constantinople where the Schism happened. Find one photograph of its interior. Write in your Field Manual: what does it feel like to look at this building knowing what happened there in 1054? This church was the center of Orthodox worship for nearly a thousand years.
sessions.reading_reference: John 17:20–23 — That They May All Be One
sessions.liturgical_connection: This Sunday at the Liturgy, listen for the prayer for the unity of all — the priest prays for the unity of the faith and the communion of the Holy Spirit at several points in the Divine Liturgy. The Orthodox Church has never stopped praying for the healing of the schisms. Point this out to your child and ask them: what do you think Christian unity would actually look like if it were restored?

sessions.title: The Reformation & Orthodoxy's Response
sessions.description: In 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther nailed a list of ninety-five complaints to the door of a church in Wittenberg. He was protesting the corruption of the Roman Catholic Church — the selling of indulgences, the power of the papacy, the distance between the clergy and the people. Luther's protest became a revolution. Within a generation, Western Christianity had shattered into dozens of competing movements — Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Anabaptist, and eventually thousands more. The Reformation remade the religious landscape of Europe and shaped the world your family lives in today. The Orthodox Church watched all of this from Constantinople. And its response was essentially this: you are both wrong. Rome added to the Apostolic faith. The Reformers subtracted from it. The Orthodox Church preserved it.
sessions.parent_note: The Reformation is sensitive material because many Orthodox families in America have Protestant relatives or Protestant friends who are serious, sincere Christians. The goal of this session is to help your child understand the Orthodox position clearly and to hold it with confidence — not contempt. The most important point: the Orthodox critique of the Reformation is not that Martin Luther was a bad person or that Protestants are not sincere Christians. It is that the structural principle of Sola Scriptura is self-defeating — it produces not unity around Scripture but endless fragmentation, because Scripture interpreted apart from Tradition and the Church produces as many readings as there are readers. The five solas discussion is theologically rich and worth real time. Each one captures something true — grace is essential, faith is essential, Christ alone saves — but in each case the word alone creates a problem that Orthodox theology does not have. Recommended video: Search Orthodox response to Protestantism or Fr. Andrew Damick Orthodoxy and Heterodoxy — his book and podcast series are the best accessible treatment of this topic.
key_concepts: Why the Reformation happened — The Western church in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries was genuinely corrupt in many of its institutional expressions. The papacy had become a political power. Indulgences — the selling of remission from punishment for sins — were theologically problematic and financially motivated. Luther's initial complaints were not unreasonable. The tragedy is that his solution — breaking from the Church entirely and establishing Scripture alone as the only authority — created more problems than it solved.

The five Reformation solas — The Reformers summarized their theology in five Latin phrases: Sola Scriptura (Scripture alone), Sola Fide (faith alone), Sola Gratia (grace alone), Solus Christus (Christ alone), Soli Deo Gloria (glory to God alone). The Orthodox response to each is not that the positive content is wrong but that the word alone is the problem. Scripture — yes, but within Holy Tradition. Faith — yes, but expressed through the sacramental life. Grace — yes, but working with human free will in the process of theosis.

The Orthodox critique of the Reformation — The Reformers made a fatal assumption: that the Church had so thoroughly corrupted the Christian faith that it had to be rebuilt from Scripture alone. But this assumes that an individual or a small group can correctly interpret Scripture apart from the living Tradition of the Church. The Orthodox response: the same Church that produced and recognized the canon of Scripture is the only legitimate interpreter of it.

The Reformers and Orthodoxy — Several Reformers attempted to correspond with Orthodox patriarchs, hoping to find allies against Rome. The most famous exchange was between the Lutheran theologians of Tübingen and Patriarch Jeremias II of Constantinople in the 1570s. After three extended exchanges, Patriarch Jeremias concluded that the Lutheran theology was incompatible with Orthodoxy and ended the correspondence politely but definitively.

Protestantism in the modern world — The Reformation produced religious freedom and individual conscience. It also produced a Christianity of ten thousand denominations, each claiming to read Scripture correctly, with no authoritative body to resolve disagreements. The Orthodox Church sees in this fragmentation the inevitable result of rejecting Holy Tradition and the authority of the Church as the interpreter of Scripture.

The Orthodox position — neither Rome nor the Reformation — The Orthodox Church is not a middle way between Catholicism and Protestantism. It is not splitting the difference. It is the original — the Church of the Apostles and the Seven Councils — which neither added as Rome did nor subtracted as the Reformers did from the Apostolic deposit of faith. This is a claim Orthodox Christians must be able to explain without arrogance and without apology.
sessions.reading_note: 2 Thessalonians 2:15 — hold to the traditions — was chosen because it is the direct biblical refutation of Sola Scriptura in its pure form. St. Paul explicitly commands the Thessalonians to hold to what was taught by spoken word as well as by letter. 1 Timothy 3:15 — the Church is the pillar and ground of truth — identifies the Church, not Scripture alone, as the custodian and interpreter of truth. These two passages together make the biblical case for why Scripture cannot be separated from the Church and Holy Tradition that produced, recognized, and interprets it.
sessions.discussion_q1: What is Sola Scriptura and what is the Orthodox response to it? Can you explain the Orthodox position in your own words without sounding dismissive of Protestants?
sessions.discussion_q2: You counted the Christian denominations in your town. What did you find? What does that diversity tell you?
sessions.discussion_q3: Luther's original complaints against Rome were not unreasonable — the Church was genuinely corrupt in many ways. Does that make the Reformation justified? How do you reform a corrupt institution without breaking it apart?
sessions.journal_prompt: In your Field Manual, write your response to this question from a Protestant friend: you say you believe in Scripture — but Protestants believe in Scripture too, and there are thousands of Protestant denominations who all disagree about what it says. What does that tell you about Scripture alone as the only rule of faith? Write your answer as if you were actually having the conversation.
sessions.family_activity: As a family, read about Patriarch Jeremias II's response to the Lutheran theologians of Tübingen — a short summary is available in many Orthodox history books and online. He writes with great charity but great clarity. Discuss: how does he manage to be both firm in the faith and genuinely respectful of those he disagrees with? What can your family learn from his example?
sessions.personal_activity: Find out what Christian denominations are present in your town or city — how many different churches of how many different traditions. Write the list in your Field Manual. Then write: what does this diversity tell you about what happens when there is no authoritative community to interpret the faith?
sessions.reading_reference: 2 Thessalonians 2:15 + 1 Timothy 3:15 — The Pillar and Ground of Truth
sessions.liturgical_connection: This Sunday at the Liturgy, notice the continuity. The prayers you are hearing are the same prayers Christians have been praying since the fourth century. The Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom is older than Luther, older than the Schism, older than most of the controversies this session covers. When you stand in an Orthodox church for the Divine Liturgy you are standing in the stream of the unbroken Apostolic faith.

sessions.title: Orthodoxy in the Modern World
sessions.description: The twentieth century was the bloodiest century in Christian history. More Christians were martyred between 1900 and 2000 than in all the previous nineteen centuries combined. In Russia alone, under the Soviet regime, tens of thousands of priests were executed, hundreds of monasteries were destroyed, and the entire machinery of a modern state was turned against the Church for seventy years. In the Middle East, ancient Christian communities that trace themselves directly to the Apostles were systematically reduced by war, displacement, and persecution. And yet the Orthodox Church survived. More than survived — it grew, spread to new continents, planted itself in the Americas and Australia and Western Europe, and produced saints and martyrs whose witness rivals anything from the early centuries. This is where the story of Church history arrives at the present moment. And the present moment is yours.
sessions.parent_note: Session 1.11 is the capstone of the entire Church History section and of Topic 1 as a whole. The goal is to bring the sweep of two thousand years of history home — literally home, to your family's kitchen table. The family activity — tracing how the faith came to your family — is potentially the most powerful activity in the entire curriculum. Take time with it. If you can call a grandparent or elder family member while doing it, do so. If you have old photographs of a church in the old country, find them. The chain of transmission is not abstract — it runs through specific people, specific parishes, specific decisions to baptize children and attend Liturgy and keep the fast. The twentieth century martyrs are important and should not be glossed over. The Russian New Martyrs in particular are among the greatest witnesses in Christian history. St. Elizabeth the New Martyr — Grand Duchess Elizabeth of Russia, who became a nun after her husband was assassinated and was eventually thrown alive into a mine shaft by the Bolsheviks — is a particularly powerful figure for children in this age range. Recommended video: Search New Martyrs of Russia or St. Elizabeth New Martyr — Ancient Faith has excellent documentary material.
key_concepts: The Russian martyrs — a new age of martyrdom — The Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 brought to power a regime explicitly committed to the elimination of religion. Patriarch Tikhon of Moscow was imprisoned. Metropolitan Benjamin of Petrograd was shot. Thousands of priests, monks, and nuns were executed or sent to labor camps. The New Martyrs and Confessors of Russia — canonized by the Russian Orthodox Church in 2000 — number in the tens of thousands. They are among the greatest cloud of witnesses in Christian history.

The Orthodox diaspora — the faith goes West — Political upheaval, war, and persecution scattered Orthodox Christians across the Western world throughout the twentieth century. Greeks, Russians, Serbs, Romanians, Arabs, and others brought their faith with them to America, Australia, and Western Europe. What began as ethnic immigrant communities has become a growing, converting, multinational Orthodox presence in the Western world. Orthodoxy is no longer simply an Eastern religion.

Orthodox missions in the modern era — St. Innocent of Alaska brought the Orthodox faith to the indigenous peoples of Alaska and Siberia in the nineteenth century, translating the Liturgy into their languages. St. Nicholas of Japan founded the Japanese Orthodox Church. In Africa, the Orthodox Church has grown rapidly. The faith of the Apostles continues to spread — not by political power but by the same person-to-person witness that always characterized authentic Christian mission.

The ecumenical movement and Orthodoxy — The twentieth century produced a significant movement toward Christian unity — the World Council of Churches and numerous bilateral dialogues between Orthodox and Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches. The Orthodox Church participates in these dialogues while maintaining that visible unity can only be achieved on the basis of the fullness of the Apostolic faith. Theological dialogue is not the same as pretending disagreements do not exist.

Orthodoxy in America — The Orthodox Church in America, the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese, the Antiochian Orthodox Archdiocese, and other jurisdictions are all part of the same Orthodox faith but exist in separate administrative structures — a legacy of the diaspora and immigration history. The question of Orthodox unity in America remains unresolved but is actively discussed. What is clear is that Orthodoxy in America is growing, converting, and increasingly present in American life.

You are part of this story — The Orthodox Expedition exists because the faith that was handed from Christ to the Apostles, preserved through persecution and heresy and schism and revolution, arrived somehow in your home. You are not at the end of this story. You are somewhere in the middle. The question Church history ultimately asks is not what happened then but what you will do now. Every generation of the Church has had to decide whether to hold the faith, pass it on, and if necessary, die for it. That question is yours too.
sessions.reading_note: Hebrews 12:1–2 was chosen as the capstone reading because it frames the entire sweep of Church history in one image — a great cloud of witnesses surrounding us, cheering us on. The martyrs, the Fathers, the confessors, the missionaries, the ordinary faithful who kept the fast and attended the Liturgy and baptized their children — all of them are present. We are not alone in this. We run the race they ran. And we fix our eyes on the same Christ they fixed their eyes on.
sessions.discussion_q1: We studied two thousand years of Church history in six sessions. What is the single most important thing you learned? What surprised you most?
sessions.discussion_q2: You looked up a twentieth century Orthodox saint or martyr. Tell me about them. What did they do with their faith? What do you want to do with yours?
sessions.discussion_q3: How did the Orthodox faith come to your family? Who passed it on? What would have been lost if someone in that chain had decided it was not worth the effort?
sessions.journal_prompt: In your Field Manual, write your answer to this question: you have now studied the entire sweep of Church history from Pentecost to the present. What is the single most important thing you have learned? And what do you believe God is asking of you — specifically you, in your time and place — as a result?
sessions.family_activity: As a family, discuss: how did the Orthodox faith come to your family? Who passed it on to whom? Go back as far as you can — grandparents, great-grandparents, the country your family came from, the parish they attended. You are the current link in a chain that goes back to the Apostles. How does that feel? What do you want to pass on?
sessions.personal_activity: Look up one Orthodox saint or martyr from the twentieth century — St. Tikhon of Moscow, St. Elizabeth the New Martyr, St. John of Shanghai, or anyone else who interests you. Read a brief account of their life. Write in your Field Manual: what did they do with their faith that you want to do with yours?
sessions.reading_reference: Hebrews 12:1–2 — Surrounded by a Cloud of Witnesses
sessions.liturgical_connection: This Sunday at the Liturgy, look around at your fellow parishioners. Each of them is part of the same unbroken chain — the faith of the Apostles, preserved through persecution and schism and revolution and diaspora, arriving in this room, in this city, on this Sunday. After the Liturgy, ask your child: if someone a hundred years from now is asking how the faith came to their family, what will they say about us?

sessions.title: What is a Sacrament?
sessions.description: A sacrament is a divine encounter with Christ — not a ritual, not a symbol, but a real meeting with the living God.
key_concepts: A sacrament = divine institution + visible sign + hidden grace of God
He who was visible as our Redeemer has now passed into the Sacraments — St. Leo the Great
Not magical rituals — they require faith and participation
The number seven is symbolic — Orthodoxy recognizes more than seven
Other sacraments: monastic profession, blessing of waters, icons, relics, prayer, charity
The purpose: to impart the life of Christ and lead us to theosis
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: What is the difference between a sacrament and a regular ritual or ceremony?

sessions.title: Baptism & Chrismation
sessions.description: The two sacraments of initiation that make us members of Christ and seal us with the Holy Spirit.
key_concepts: Baptism — dying and rising with Christ in water, cleansing of sin
Three immersions — in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
Chrismation — personal Pentecost, sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit
The three sacraments of initiation: Baptism, Chrismation, Eucharist together
Administered together in Orthodox Church — unlike Western churches
We are made children of God and temples of the Holy Spirit
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Describe what you think happened spiritually when you were baptized.

sessions.title: The Holy Eucharist
sessions.description: The center of Orthodox worship — the real presence of Christ in the bread and wine, Body and Blood.
key_concepts: The Eucharist is a personal encounter with the living Christ
Jesus is truly present — not symbolic, not a memorial only
We are in the Upper Room with the Apostles at every Liturgy
The Holy Spirit consecrates the gifts — the same Spirit that formed Jesus in Mary
Preparation: self-examination, fasting, prayer, pre-communion prayers
Man was created to contain God — we are temples of His presence
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: What does it mean to you that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist?

sessions.title: Holy Confession
sessions.description: The sacrament of healing — not punishment. Christ comes to liberate and heal the sinner, not condemn.
key_concepts: Confession is the Second Baptism — forgiveness of all sins after Baptism
Christ stands invisible — the priest is only the witness
Healing not punishment — the sinner is a prisoner of Satan, not a criminal before a judge
Theology of tears — St. John Climacus on weeping for sins
Two kinds: private prayer confession nightly, sacramental confession before a priest
Always followed by Holy Communion — the blood of Christ washes away sin
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Why do you think God uses a priest for confession instead of just praying directly?

sessions.title: Holy Orders
sessions.description: The sacrament by which God calls men to shepherd His Church — the unbroken chain from Christ to today.
key_concepts: Jesus ordained the Apostles who ordained others in an unbroken chain
Three orders: deacon, priest, bishop
Ordination by the laying on of hands and prayer
Apostolic Succession — the unbroken historical link to Christ and the Apostles
This proves the Church is authentically the one Church founded by Christ
A bishop's ordination requires at least two other bishops
sessions.journal_prompt: Draw the Apostolic Succession as a chain in your field journal — starting with Christ and ending with your priest.

sessions.title: Holy Matrimony
sessions.description: Marriage is a sacrament — God blessing love, making it possible to love as He loves.
key_concepts: Marriage is not a social arrangement — it is a sacrament, the oldest of God's institutions
Without me you can do nothing — Christ must be in the center
St. Paul calls marriage a Mystery in Ephesians 5
The crowning ceremony — crowned as king and queen of their own small kingdom
Marriage helps both spouses grow toward God — salvation together
The Church's approach to divorce — oikonomia, not approval
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Why do you think God designed marriage to include Him in the center?

sessions.title: Holy Unction
sessions.description: The sacrament of healing — God's care for the whole person, body and soul together.
key_concepts: Jesus gave the Apostles power to heal — Mark 6:13, Luke 9:1-2
James 5:13-15 — the biblical command to anoint the sick
The body is not evil — it is a temple of God destined for heaven
Celebrated every Holy Wednesday evening at SJTD
God does not always promise healing but always promises salvation
We are healed to bring healing to others — like the Good Samaritan
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: What does it mean that your body is a temple of God?

sessions.title: Living the Sacramental Life
sessions.description: How all the sacraments connect and what it means to build a life around them day by day.
key_concepts: The sacraments are not one-time events — they build a lifelong rhythm
Regular confession and communion — the heartbeat of Orthodox life
A healthy rhythm: confession before each communion season
The sacraments connect to every part of life — morning prayer, fasting, feast days
The domestic church — the family as a small church
Every baptized person is called to become a saint through the sacramental life
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: What would a week in your life look like if you built it around the sacraments?

sessions.title: The Theotokos — Mother of God
sessions.description: Who Mary is, why the Orthodox Church honors her above all saints, and what she means for our faith.
key_concepts: Theotokos means God-bearer — defined at Council of Ephesus 431
Her life: dedication to temple at age 3, perpetual virginity, annunciation
The New Eve — her yes to God reverses Eve's no
We ask her to pray for us — we do not pray to her as God
She is always shown pointing to Christ — her whole life directs us to Him
Her many names: Panagia, Aeiparthenos, Queen of Heaven, Heavenly Ladder
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: Why is it important that we call Mary the Mother of God and not just the mother of Jesus?

sessions.title: The Saints & Relics
sessions.description: The saints are alive in Christ and cheer us on. Their relics are holy because their bodies were temples of the Holy Spirit.
key_concepts: Saints are alive in Christ — Hebrews 12:1-2, the cloud of witnesses
We ask saints to pray for us — not pray to them as God
Christ is the only mediator — saints are intercessors, like asking a friend to pray
Three classes of relics: body parts, items used, items touched
Biblical basis: Elisha's bones, Paul's handkerchiefs, Jesus' garment
Veneration is not worship — God is glorified through His saints
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Who is your patron saint? Write their name and one thing about their life.

sessions.title: The Holy Angels
sessions.description: The angelic hosts who serve God, guard us, and fill the Divine Liturgy — our constant unseen companions.
key_concepts: Angels are spiritual beings created by God before the visible world
The nine angelic ranks: Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, Angels
Three Archangels: Michael (commander of heavenly armies), Gabriel (messenger of God), Raphael (healer sent by God)
Every Orthodox Christian has a guardian angel
Angels are present at every Divine Liturgy — the Cherubic Hymn
We ask our guardian angel to pray for us in morning and evening prayers
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: Draw the three Archangels and write one thing about each one.

sessions.title: Iconography — Windows to Heaven
sessions.description: Icons are not decorations — they are theology written in color. Every element has meaning.
key_concepts: Icons are open books to remind us of God — St. John of Damascus
St. Luke wrote the first icon of the Theotokos — Hodegetria, One Who Shows the Way
Everything in an icon has meaning: colors, objects, halos, reverse perspective
Color meanings: gold = divine light, blue = heavenly, red = martyrdom or royalty, white = purity and resurrection
Iconoclasm 726-843 — persecution of icon venerators, Empress Irene restores icons
Sunday of Orthodoxy — first Sunday of Great Lent, victory of icons since 843
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Find one icon in your home or church and describe what you see. What colors are used? What does the person look like?

sessions.title: The Church Building — A Map of Heaven
sessions.description: Every part of an Orthodox church is theology made visible. The building itself teaches the faith.
key_concepts: The Narthex — the entrance, where catechumens stood, space of preparation
The Nave — where the faithful gather, representing the world redeemed
The Iconostasis — the boundary between heaven and earth, not a wall but a door
The Royal Doors — Christ as the door to the Kingdom
The Sanctuary and Altar — the Kingdom of God, where the sacrifice is offered
The High Place — where the bishop sits, representing Christ as head of the Church
sessions.journal_prompt: Sketch a simple map of your church in your field journal and label each section.

sessions.title: Liturgical Objects & Vestments
sessions.description: The holy objects used in worship and what each one represents — every item tells a story.
key_concepts: The Chalice — the cup of the Eucharist, the blood of Christ
The Diskos — the plate holding the Lamb, representing the manger at Bethlehem
The Spear and Sponge — recalling the crucifixion
The Holy Gospel Book — Christ present as the Word of God
The Censer and Incense — prayers rising to God like incense, Psalm 141
Vestment colors: gold (general), blue (Theotokos), red (martyrs), green (Palm Sunday/Pentecost), purple (Lent), white (Pascha)
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Draw the censer and write what the incense and smoke represents.

sessions.title: Liturgical Gestures & Church Etiquette
sessions.description: How to worship with your whole body — the sign of the cross, prostrations, veneration, and receiving communion.
key_concepts: The Sign of the Cross — right to left, thumb and first two fingers together representing Trinity
Metanias — small bow with hand to floor, full prostrations on weekdays in Lent
Kissing icons — veneration passes to the person depicted, not the wood and paint
Candles — our prayer made visible, the light of Christ in the darkness
Why we stand — resurrection posture, we stand as those risen with Christ
Receiving Holy Communion — hands crossed on chest, mouth open, receive on spoon, never chew
sessions.journal_prompt: Practice the Sign of the Cross three times correctly and write in your field journal how it felt different from before this lesson.

sessions.title: The Divine Services
sessions.description: The Orthodox Church prays around the clock — the daily cycle of services that sanctifies every hour.
key_concepts: The Hours — each a three-hour watch corresponding to events of the Passion
1st Hour 6AM — sanctifies the breaking day
3rd Hour 9AM — descent of Holy Spirit at Pentecost
6th Hour 12PM — the Crucifixion of Christ
9th Hour 3PM — the death of Jesus and taking down from the Cross
Vespers — liturgical day begins at sunset, following Genesis
Compline — after dinner service, asking protection during sleep
Orthros/Matins — morning service, Magnificat, Great Doxology
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: Which of the daily services would you most like to attend and why?

sessions.title: The Divine Liturgy Part 1 — Liturgy of the Catechumens
sessions.description: The first half of the Liturgy — gathering, proclaiming the Word, and preparing the faithful.
key_concepts: Liturgy means common work — the action of the whole Church together
Prothesis — preparation of the bread and wine before Liturgy begins
Blessed is the Kingdom — the opening declaration of what the Liturgy is about
The Great Litany — all-embracing prayer, Lord have mercy
The Small Entrance — solemn procession with the Gospel Book
The Epistle and Gospel — sacramental proclamation of the Word of God
The Fervent Supplication — prayers for our needs and the world
sessions.journal_prompt: Draw the Small Entrance procession in your field journal and label what the priest is carrying and why.

sessions.title: The Divine Liturgy Part 2 — Liturgy of the Faithful
sessions.description: The second half of the Liturgy — the offering, the consecration, and the reception of Holy Communion.
key_concepts: The Great Entrance — offertory procession, symbolizes Palm Sunday, Cherubic Hymn
The Kiss of Peace — let us love one another
The Creed — The Doors! The Doors! — personal confession of baptismal faith
The Anaphora — the Eucharistic Canon, lifting up to God
The Epiklesis — calling down the Holy Spirit to consecrate the gifts
Holy Communion — Holy Things are for the Holy!, received on a spoon
The Dismissal — go forth to bear witness to the Kingdom in the world
sessions.journal_prompt: Write the Liturgy sequence in your field journal from memory — try to list at least 8 parts in order.

sessions.title: Prayer — Types & Purpose
sessions.description: What Orthodox prayer actually is, why we pray, and the four types of prayer in the Church.
key_concepts: All Orthodox prayer is Trinitarian — to the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit
Prayer is the lifting of mind and heart to God — walking in His presence
Four types: petition (asking), thanksgiving (gratitude), lamentation (crying out), adoration (praising)
We also pray to the saints as intercessors — asking them to pray for us
Personal prayer at home is different from communal prayer at church
The purpose of prayer: communion with God and conformity to His will
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Write one short prayer for each of the four types — petition, thanksgiving, lamentation, adoration.

sessions.title: The Jesus Prayer & The Komboskini
sessions.description: The ancient prayer of the heart — Lord Jesus Christ Son of God have mercy on me a sinner.
key_concepts: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner
Based on the prayer of the blind man in the Gospels — Luke 18:38
Praying without ceasing — 1 Thessalonians 5:17
The Komboskini — prayer rope, each knot tied with a cross, used to count repetitions
The prayer calms the mind and draws attention to God throughout the day
Hesychasm — the tradition of interior stillness and prayer of the heart
Used by monks and laypeople alike throughout Orthodox history
sessions.journal_prompt: Practice the Jesus Prayer 10 times with your komboskini or by counting on your fingers. Write in your field journal how it felt.

sessions.title: The Home Prayer Rule
sessions.description: Building a family prayer life at home — the Orthodox tradition of morning and evening prayer.
key_concepts: Morning prayers — begin the day consecrated to God
Evening prayers — end the day with thanksgiving and asking forgiveness
The Orthodox Prayer Book — prayers written by the Church Fathers
Why we pray set prayers — the Church's wisdom shapes our prayer life
Setting up a home prayer corner — icons, candle, incense
Mealtime prayers — blessing food as a eucharistic act
The family that prays together — the home as domestic church
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Design your ideal home prayer corner. Where would it be? What icons would you include?

sessions.title: Following the Liturgy — The Responses
sessions.description: Learning to actively participate in the Liturgy by knowing and saying the responses.
key_concepts: Kyrie Eleison — Lord have mercy, the fundamental prayer of the Liturgy
Lord have mercy — said 3, 12, and 40 times in different litanies
Grant this O Lord — response to petitions
And with your spirit — response to the priest's greeting
Axios — He is worthy — the people's affirmation at ordination
Amen — so be it, the people's seal on every prayer
The Liturgy is not done for you but by you — active participation
sessions.journal_prompt: Write all 5 liturgical responses in your field journal in English. Next Sunday, try to say them out loud.

sessions.title: Greek in the Liturgy
sessions.description: Key Greek words and phrases heard every Sunday — what they mean and why they matter.
key_concepts: Kyrie Eleison — Lord have mercy (Κύριε ἐλέησον)
Christos Anesti — Christ is Risen (Χριστὸς Ἀνέστη)
Alithos Anesti — Truly He is Risen (Ἀληθῶς Ἀνέστη)
Doxa si o Theos — Glory to You O God (Δόξα σοι ὁ Θεός)
Axios — He is worthy (Ἄξιος)
Eis polla eti Despota — Many years Master (Εἰς πολλὰ ἔτη δέσποτα)
Theotokos — God-bearer (Θεοτόκος)
Greek is the language of the New Testament and Byzantine civilization
sessions.journal_prompt: Write the 7 Greek phrases from this lesson in your field journal with their English meaning.

sessions.title: Preparing for & Departing from Liturgy
sessions.description: How to prepare your heart before Liturgy and give thanks after — the Liturgy does not end at the dismissal.
key_concepts: The night before — pre-communion prayers, early to bed
Morning of Liturgy — fast from food and water, morning prayers
Arriving early — veneration of icons, candles, quiet preparation
During Liturgy — stand attentively, follow along, make responses
Receiving Communion — hands crossed, receive on spoon, never chew, kiss the chalice base
After Liturgy — antidoron, post-communion prayers, take the Liturgy into the week
The dismissal is a sending — go forth to be the Church in the world
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Write three things you want to do differently at Liturgy after this lesson.

sessions.title: Liturgical Books & Orthodox Resources at Home
sessions.description: The books the Church uses, good Orthodox resources for home, and how to follow the calendar at home.
key_concepts: The Horologion — the Book of Hours for the daily services
The Menaion — hymns for the fixed feasts of each month
The Triodion — services from the Sunday of the Publican through Holy Saturday
The Pentecostarion — services from Pascha to the Sunday of All Saints
The Orthodox Study Bible — recommended translation for home reading
Ancient Faith Radio — podcasts, music, resources for Orthodox families
Antiochian Archdiocese and GOA websites for calendar and resources
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: What is one Orthodox resource you want to explore this week?

sessions.title: Feasts & The Church Calendar
sessions.description: The Orthodox year is a journey through the whole life of Christ — a living theological school.
key_concepts: The church year begins September 1st and is based on the Julian calendar
Pascha — the Feast of Feasts, the Resurrection, the center of everything
The 12 Great Feasts: 7 Lord's feasts + 5 Theotokos feasts
Lord's Feasts: Exaltation of Cross, Christmas, Theophany, Palm Sunday, Ascension, Pentecost, Transfiguration
Theotokos Feasts: Birth, Entry into Temple, Presentation of Christ, Annunciation, Dormition
Vestment colors mark the season visually every Sunday
sessions.journal_prompt: Draw the church year as a wheel in your field journal with Pascha at the center. Mark the 12 Great Feasts around the outside.

sessions.title: Great Lent & The Sundays of Lent
sessions.description: The great fast of preparation for Pascha — a season of repentance, not just giving things up.
key_concepts: Great Lent is about repentance and permanent change — not temporary sacrifice
Pre-Lenten Sundays: Publican and Pharisee, Prodigal Son, Last Judgment, Forgiveness Sunday
1st Sunday of Lent: Sunday of Orthodoxy — victory of icons
2nd Sunday: St. Gregory Palamas — hesychasm and uncreated light
3rd Sunday: Veneration of the Holy Cross — midpoint, perseverance
4th Sunday: St. John Climacus — the Ladder of Divine Ascent
5th Sunday: St. Mary of Egypt — transformation and repentance
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: What is one thing you want to change permanently — not just give up for Lent?

sessions.title: Holy Week — Day by Day at SJTD
sessions.description: The most important week of the year — every day, every service, every moment points to the Resurrection.
key_concepts: Palm Sunday — Christ enters Jerusalem, the Lenten fast ends, Holy Week begins
Holy Monday & Tuesday — Bridegroom services, readings on betrayal and repentance
Holy Tuesday — the Hymn of Kassiani, chanted only this one night of the year
Holy Wednesday — Holy Unction at SJTD (children's and evening), remembering Judas
Holy Thursday — Liturgy, Passion service with 12 Gospel readings, Last Supper
Holy Friday — Royal Hours, unnailing service, Lamentations and procession around the church
Holy Saturday — 15 OT readings, Paschal Vigil at 11pm, Christ is Risen at midnight
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: Which Holy Week service do you want to attend this year and why?

sessions.title: Fasting — Exterior & Interior
sessions.description: Orthodox fasting is both physical and spiritual — what we eat and what we think and say.
key_concepts: When to fast: Wednesday and Friday most weeks, plus 4 yearly fasting seasons
4 Fasting Seasons: Great Lent + Holy Week, Apostles' Fast, Dormition Fast (Aug 1-14), Nativity Fast (Nov 15-Dec 24)
Exterior fasting: abstaining from animal products, wine, oil on strict fast days
Why no blood products — Christ shed His blood for us
Interior fasting: negative thinking, harmful speech, what we see and hear
Isaiah 58:6-11 — true fasting means helping others
Fasting and prayer are always paired — never one without the other
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: What is one interior thing you could fast from this week alongside any food fasting?

sessions.title: Feasting & The Rhythm of the Year
sessions.description: The genius of the Orthodox calendar — you cannot understand the feasts without the fasts, and the fasts without the feasts.
key_concepts: Every fast leads to a feast — Nativity Fast leads to Christmas, Great Lent leads to Pascha
Feast days are not always a break from fasting — Exaltation of Cross is always a fast day
The liturgical year at home — marking feasts and fasts as a family
Vestment colors as a visual calendar — noticing what the priest wears
Pentecost — 50 days after Pascha, descent of Holy Spirit, establishment of the Church
Ascension — 40 days after Pascha, the Great Commission
The church year teaches theology without you even realizing it
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Mark the next three feast days coming up and write one sentence about each one.

sessions.title: Name Days, Patron Saints & Family Feast Days
sessions.description: Name days are more important than birthdays in Orthodox tradition — honoring the saint whose name you bear.
key_concepts: Your name day is the feast day of your patron saint
Name days are more important than birthdays in Greek Orthodox culture
How to find your name day — the Orthodox calendar
Celebrating name days: church if possible, family gathering, special meal
Your patron saint prays for you specifically — a heavenly protector
Family feast days — celebrating the feasts of saints the family is devoted to
Philotimo — the Greek concept of honor and generosity, lived out in these celebrations
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Write your patron saint's name, feast day, and one thing about their life.

sessions.title: Spiritual Gifts & Almsgiving
sessions.description: The Holy Spirit gives each of us gifts not for ourselves but for the building up of others.
key_concepts: The Holy Spirit is given at Chrismation — sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit
Fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control
Charismata — spiritual gifts: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues, interpretation
Love is the greatest gift — 1 Corinthians 13
Almsgiving is philanthropy of the heart — not just giving money but giving yourself
We are called to be Paracletes — comforters, advocates, helpers like the Holy Spirit
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Which spiritual gift do you think you might have? How could you use it to help others?

sessions.title: Sin & Repentance
sessions.description: Sin is missing the mark — and repentance is the joyful turn back toward God.
key_concepts: Sin means missing the mark — like an arrow that misses its target
The Fall broke communion with God — sin continues that break
Sin, evil, suffering, and death always go together — Romans 5:12
Repentance (metanoia) means change of mind — turning around completely
Repentance is positive not negative — looking upward at God's love not downward at failures
Not what we failed to be but what by grace we can now become — Met. Kallistos Ware
This life has been given to us for repentance — St. Isaac the Syrian
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: What does it mean to you that repentance is positive — looking upward not downward?

sessions.title: Sacred Music
sessions.description: Byzantine chant is theology you can sing — the oral catechism of the Orthodox Church.
key_concepts: Byzantine chant: monophonic (one voice or melody), no instruments, ancient neumes notation
8 modes — each with a distinct mood, shifting with the liturgical season
Three purposes: worship of God, education (oral catechism), transformation (lifting mind to God)
Troparion — short hymn, the Paschal Troparion is the most famous: Christ is Risen
Kontakion — extended verse hymn, the Christmas Kontakion by St. Roman the Melodist
Canon — 9 odes based on Biblical canticles, used at Matins and Compline
Paschal Troparion in Greek: Christos Anesti ek nekron, thanato thanaton patisas
sessions.journal_prompt: Write the Paschal Troparion in English in your field journal. Begin memorizing it this week.

sessions.title: Theosis — The Goal of Orthodox Life
sessions.description: Theosis is the Orthodox word for the ultimate goal — becoming by grace what God is by nature.
key_concepts: Theosis means becoming by grace what God is by nature — not becoming God but sharing His divine life
God became man so that man might become God — St. Athanasius
Synergy — we cooperate with God's grace, we do not earn theosis
The saints are examples of theosis lived out in human history
The sacraments, prayer, fasting, and almsgiving are all paths toward theosis
Orthodoxy is profoundly optimistic about human nature — we can truly be transformed
Theosis is not for after death — it begins now in this life
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Write what theosis means in your own words — as if explaining it to a friend.

sessions.title: The Virtues & The Passions
sessions.description: The inner life of the Orthodox Christian — what we are fighting against and what we are growing toward.
key_concepts: The passions are not emotions — they are disordered attachments that pull us away from God
The eight logismoi (thoughts): gluttony, lust, greed, sadness, anger, acedia (listlessness), vainglory, pride
Each passion has a corresponding virtue to overcome it
Nepsis — watchfulness, guarding the heart and mind
Practical asceticism: fasting, prayer, almsgiving, and silence as tools against the passions
The goal is not to crush emotions but to order them rightly toward God
The saints are our examples of virtues lived out
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Which of the eight passions do you think is hardest to fight? Which virtue is its opposite?

sessions.title: The Philokalia & The Spiritual Life
sessions.description: The great treasury of Orthodox spiritual wisdom — the inner life is a serious expedition.
key_concepts: The Philokalia means love of the beautiful — a collection of Orthodox spiritual writings
Compiled by St. Nikodimos of the Holy Mountain and St. Makarios of Corinth
Covers watchfulness, prayer of the heart, guarding the mind, and the spiritual life
The neptic tradition — interior attentiveness as the foundation of Orthodox spirituality
The Way of the Pilgrim — a famous Russian story about the Jesus Prayer
The spiritual life requires a guide — the role of the father confessor
Orthodox Christianity is not just external practice — it is transformation from within
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: What does it mean to guard your heart and mind? What would that look like in your daily life?

sessions.title: Martyrdom & Confession of Faith
sessions.description: The martyrs built the Church with their blood. What does it mean to confess your faith?
key_concepts: Martyr means witness — the martyrs witnessed to Christ with their lives
The blood of martyrs is the seed of the Church — Tertullian
St. Ignatius of Antioch — chose death over denying Christ, said he was wheat ground by lions
St. Polycarp of Smyrna — 86 years I have served Him and He has never done me wrong
The New Martyrs of Russia — those who died under Communist persecution in the 20th century
St. Kosmas Aitolos — Greek martyr and missionary to the Ottoman-occupied Greeks
What would you do? — Confessing the faith in daily life, not just in persecution
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: Why do you think the martyrs chose death rather than denying Christ? What does their example mean for your life?

sessions.title: Being Part of the Church — One Body
sessions.description: We work out our salvation together. Orthodoxy is never private — it is always communal.
key_concepts: We are one body in Christ — 1 Corinthians 12, branches grafted into the Vine
Salvation is not individual — we are saved together as the people of God
The fall of one weakens the whole — St. Gregory the Theologian
Ministry and stewardship — using our gifts and resources for the Church
The Orthodox phronema — the Orthodox mind and way of seeing the world
Living Orthodoxy in a non-Orthodox world — being salt and light
Engaging with the parish community — SJTD ministries and opportunities
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: What is one way you can contribute to your church community this year?

sessions.title: Death & Orthodox Burial
sessions.description: Death is not the end — it is a passage. The Orthodox funeral is a service of hope not despair.
