key_concepts: Death is a passage not an ending — the soul continues
The Orthodox funeral service — a Divine Liturgy for the departed
Why we bury the body — the body is sacred, a temple of the Holy Spirit
The Trisagion — short memorial service said at the graveside and in church
The body is laid facing east — toward the rising sun, symbol of the Resurrection
The white vestments of the funeral — hope of the Resurrection
Death comes to everyone — the Orthodox approach is honest and hopeful
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Write what you think happens when a person dies, based on what you have learned about Orthodox faith.

sessions.title: Memorial Services & Praying for the Dead
sessions.description: The Church prays for the departed — because we are one body and death does not break communion.
key_concepts: Parastas — the full memorial service for the departed
Trisagion — the short memorial prayer said at the grave or in church
Saturday of Souls — special Saturdays throughout the year for all the departed
Koliva — the boiled wheat offered at memorials, symbolizing the grain that dies to bear fruit (John 12:24)
Why we pray for the dead — the Church is one body including those who have departed
We ask the saints to pray for us — the prayer of the living for the dead is the same logic
The 40-day, 3-month, and yearly memorials — Orthodox tradition
sessions.journal_prompt: Write in your field journal: Why do you think it matters to pray for people who have already died?

sessions.title: The Soul After Death & Judgment
sessions.description: What happens to the soul after death — the particular judgment and the intermediate state.
key_concepts: The soul is immediately judged after death — the particular judgment
The soul goes to a place of rest (Paradise) or a place of separation from God
Hades is not the same as Hell — it is the intermediate state before the final judgment
The prayers of the living can help those in the intermediate state
The toll-houses — a traditional image for the soul's journey, understood as a teaching not literal doctrine
We do not know the final state of any specific person — only God judges
The mercy of God is beyond our understanding — we pray and trust
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: What questions do you still have about what happens after death?

sessions.title: The Second Coming & The Kingdom of God
sessions.description: Christ will come again — the resurrection of the body, the final judgment, and the new creation.
key_concepts: The Second Coming — Christ will return visibly, in glory, to judge the living and the dead
The resurrection of the body — our physical bodies will be raised and reunited with our souls
The general judgment — all of humanity judged together at the end of time
The Kingdom of God — a transformed creation, not a disembodied heaven
The new heaven and new earth — Revelation 21, all things made new
All of Orthodox life points forward to this moment
We live in the end times — every Liturgy is a foretaste of the Kingdom
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: What do you think the Kingdom of God will be like? Draw or describe it.

sessions.title: Hope & The Resurrection — Christ Changes Everything
sessions.description: The Resurrection of Christ is the foundation of everything — not just a doctrine but a lived reality.
key_concepts: Christ is Risen from the dead, trampling down death by death — the Paschal Troparion
The Resurrection is not a metaphor — it is the most important fact in history
Every Sunday is a little Pascha — the Resurrection is celebrated every week
The Resurrection changes how we see death, suffering, and evil
We are an Easter people — our whole life is shaped by the empty tomb
St. Paul: if Christ has not been raised your faith is futile — 1 Corinthians 15
The Resurrection is the answer to everything in this curriculum
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Write a letter to someone who has never heard of the Resurrection. Explain why it matters and what it changes.

sessions.title: Greek Orthodox Culture & Philotimo
sessions.description: What makes Greek Orthodox life and culture distinctive — and what philotimo means for how we live.
key_concepts: Philotimo — untranslatable Greek word: love of honor, doing right because it is right
Greek Orthodox culture: warm, communal, food-centered, family-first
Coffee hour after Liturgy — not just coffee, it is community and belonging
Name days celebrated more than birthdays in Greek culture
Food and fasting as cultural practice — traditional Lenten foods
The Greek family — how faith and family are intertwined in Greek Orthodox life
What it means to be Orthodox and Greek in America
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: Write what philotimo means and give one example of how you could show it this week.

sessions.title: St. Photios Shrine — Field Expedition
sessions.description: A visit to the only Greek Orthodox national shrine in the United States — right in our backyard.
key_concepts: St. Photios of Constantinople — Patriarch, theologian, defender of Orthodoxy against the Filioque
The shrine commemorates the first Greeks in America landing in New Smyrna Beach, Florida in 1768
The Byzantine chapel — full iconography, a sacred space to experience
The museum — history of Greek Orthodox Christians in America
Connection to Topic 1 — St. Photios fought the same Filioque battle we studied
Field assignment: identify 5 icons, sketch the chapel layout, write field journal entry
Located in St. Augustine, Florida — our local sacred site
sessions.journal_prompt: After your visit, write a full field journal entry: What did you see? What surprised you? What connected to something you learned?

sessions.title: Parish Visit — A Different Jurisdiction
sessions.description: Visit a non-Greek Orthodox parish and discover that the faith is one even when the expression differs.
key_concepts: The Orthodox Church is universal — same faith expressed in many languages and cultures
Different jurisdictions: Greek, Antiochian, Russian, OCA, Serbian, Romanian, Bulgarian
What is the same everywhere: the Liturgy structure, the Creed, the Sacraments, the icons
What differs: language of worship, music style, cultural customs, calendar sometimes
The Liturgy is recognizable even in a foreign language — the structure is the same
Assignment: identify 5 things that are the same as SJTD, note 3 things that differ
We are one Church — jurisdictional differences are not divisions of faith
sessions.journal_prompt: Write a field journal comparison: How was the parish you visited the same as SJTD? How was it different? What did you think of the difference?

sessions.title: Greek in the Church & Daily Life — A Celebration
sessions.description: A joyful review of the Greek language of Orthodox worship — you know more than you think.
key_concepts: Review all Greek phrases from Session 5.8 and throughout the year
The Greek alphabet — the letters behind the familiar liturgical abbreviations
IC XC — Jesus Christ (on the diskos and in icons)
MP OY — Mother of God (Theotokos abbreviation on icons)
NIKA — He conquers (on the seal of the Lamb)
Axios — said three times at an ordination
A full year of Liturgy has taught you more Greek than you realize
sessions.journal_prompt: In your field journal: List every Greek word or phrase you now know. Write the English meaning next to each one.

sessions.title: Looking Back — What Did We Discover?
sessions.description: A family review of the full Orthodox Expedition — revisiting the field journal, the highlights, and the journey.
key_concepts: Flip through the complete field journal together as a family
Revisit the favorite moment from each topic
What surprised you most across the whole expedition?
What was the hardest topic and why?
What changed in how you see your faith and your Sunday Liturgy?
What do you still want to learn — the expedition never truly ends
Preview the Grand Presentation
sessions.journal_prompt: Write a final summary entry in your field journal: What are the three most important things you learned this year?

sessions.title: The Grand Presentation
sessions.description: The explorer presents what he has learned — his testimony, in his own words, to his family.
key_concepts: Prepare a 10-15 minute presentation for your family
Cover: what the Orthodox Expedition was
The topic that meant the most to you and why
Something that genuinely surprised you about the faith
Something you still want to keep learning about
What it means to you personally to be Orthodox
This is not a test — it is a testimony. There are no wrong answers.
sessions.journal_prompt: Write the outline of your Grand Presentation in your field journal before the presentation day.
